title: Field goals: how long the kick really is, how often it's made, and why misses swing games (and bets)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: its last update is still Oct 12, with one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. It takes the concept that decided more games this weekend than any other: the kicking game. Oregon missed three field goals and lost by 11; South Carolina, Minnesota and the Browns won on last-play or late kicks; Texas blocked one; Michigan forced overtime with one at 0:00.

The big idea: a field goal is worth 3 points, but its real value depends on distance, and distance isn't where the ball is. Every kick is 17 yards longer than the yard line it's snapped from. Past about 50 yards, a college kick is a coin flip and an NFL kick is about 7 in 10, so a coach at the opponent's 33–40 is choosing between a shaky kick, a punt that gains little, and going for it on 4th down.

White = NFL, yellow = college. The make rates are rounded, approximate league-wide figures from recent seasons, to show the shape (they fall fast past 50 yards); individual kickers vary a lot.

  1. How long is the kick (top of the diagram)? Add 7 yards for the snap back to the holder and 10 for the end zone, because the goalposts stand on the back line of the end zone. Snapped from the 35 → a 52-yarder. Thursday night, Chicago's Cairo Santos made a career-long 58 (snapped from the 41) with 1:34 left, after missing from 53. Extra points use the same math: the NFL snaps them from the 15 (a 33-yard kick; the 49ers' Eddy Pineiro missed one Sunday, his fourth miss of the season), college from the 3 (a 20-yard kick).
  2. How often they're made (bottom). NFL kickers make almost everything inside 40 and roughly 7 in 10 from 50+. College kickers are less consistent, and the field is harder: college hash marks are 40 feet apart versus the NFL's 18 feet 6 inches, so a college ball spotted on a hash leaves the kicker a sharper angle. That's why a college coach treats a 52-yarder like a gamble, and why Oregon's Gage Hurych missing from 52, 52 and 39 wasn't shocking on the long ones, only on the 39. Those 9 points were the game: Illinois won 21-10.
  3. The "no man's land" decision. Snapped between the opponent's 33 and 40, a kick is 50–57 yards. A miss gives the ball away: in the NFL at the spot of the kick (7 yards behind the line, so a miss from the 35 gives the opponent the ball at its 42), in college at the line of scrimmage. A punt from there gains maybe 20–25 yards. That's why coaches go for it on 4th-and-short in that zone (Lesson 18's third-down setup matters most here), and why a strong-legged kicker changes the math.
  4. Blocks: the 1.3-second clock. Snap, hold and kick take roughly 1.3 seconds. If the defense pushes the middle of the line back or a rusher gets a hand up, a low kick gets blocked, and a blocked kick is a live ball (Lesson 29). Saturday, Texas's Alex January blocked an Ole Miss field goal with the game tied late; Texas then kicked a 33-yarder for a 10-point lead and won by 7.
  5. Walk-off kicks and the two-minute drill. The point of a late drive is often just getting into range (Lesson 34): South Carolina's Malik Orsan won from 48 after a Tennessee fumble (27-24); Minnesota's Luke Drzewiecki won from 31 after an interception (13-10 over Iowa); Cleveland's Andre Szmyt beat Tennessee 27-24 at the gun; Michigan's Trey Butkowski tied Indiana from 26 at 0:00. Field goals are why so many games end on 3-point margins (Market 101, Lesson 2).
  6. For your bets. Every missed kick takes 3 points off the total and off the margin. Oregon's misses kept that game at 31 points (Under 51.5) and let Illinois +12.5 win outright. Field goals instead of touchdowns are also how Unders cash (Lesson 12, the red zone). Before a bet, check the kickers: the Rams changed kickers this week (Brandon McManus for Blake Grupe), and a kicker with four missed extra points is a small but real risk for a spread near 3.

How to log it in your drill: don't log the kick itself; it isn't a run or a pass. Log the snap before it. When a team already in field-goal range faces 3rd down late in a half, the most common call is a run between the hash marks to center the ball for the kicker and run clock: call RUN. When a team stays on the field on 4th-and-short at the opponent's 33–40 (no man's land), it's a go-for-it play: 4th-and-1 is mostly a run or a quarterback sneak (Lesson 33), 4th-and-4 or more is usually a pass. Fake field goals exist but are rare; don't guess them.

Real examples to look for: Sunday night in Seattle (Mon 9:20 a.m. JST / Sun 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC), a game with a 42.5 total where field goals could decide the Under; and Monday night in Philadelphia (Tue 9:15 a.m. JST / Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC). Watch where each drive stalls and do the "+17" math before the kick.

Video: search YouTube for "Cairo Santos 58 yard field goal Patriots," "Alex January blocked field goal Ole Miss Texas," "Andre Szmyt game winning field goal Titans," and "field goal hash marks college vs NFL explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: The ball is snapped from the opponent's 30. How long is the field goal?
quiz.w: 30 + 7 (the holder is 7 yards back) + 10 (the goalposts are at the back of the end zone) = 47.

quiz.q: Why are college field goals harder than NFL kicks from the same distance?
o: College hash marks are 40 feet apart (NFL 18 ft 6 in), so many kicks come from a sharper angle
College goalposts are 10 yards farther back
College kickers can't use a holder
quiz.w: The wider college hashes put the ball farther from the middle, so the angle is tougher. College kickers are also younger and less consistent.

quiz.q: An NFL team misses a 52-yarder snapped from the 35. Where does the other team take over?
o: At the 35, the line of scrimmage
At the 42, the spot of the kick
quiz.w: NFL rule: the spot of the kick, 7 yards behind the line, so the 42. In college it would be the line of scrimmage, the 35.

quiz.q: Oregon missed kicks of 52, 52 and 39 and lost 21-10 as a 12.5-point favorite. What does that mean for bets?
o: Missed kicks don't affect totals or spreads
Each miss took 3 points off the total and the margin: it helped the Under (31 points vs. 51.5) and Illinois +12.5 won outright
The game would have been a push
quiz.w: Three makes would have meant 40 points and an Oregon deficit of 2: still an Illinois cover, but a very different game script. Kicks move totals and margins 3 points at a time.
